newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: UN court to deliver war crimes verdict on May 7.
newsitem.headline: UN court to deliver war crimes verdict on May 7.

text.p: The U.N. Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia said on Tuesday it would deliver its verdict in the war crimes trial of Bosnian Serb Dusan "Dusko" Tadic on May 7, a year to the day after it began.
The trial, during which more than 100 witnesses appeared before the Hague-based court, ended in November last year.
Since then, the panel of three judges led by Gabrielle Kirk McDonald of the United States have been considering their verdict.
Tadic, a 41-year-old former cafe owner and father of two girls, is charged with committing atrocities against Moslems during the "ethnic cleansing" of northwest Bosnia by Serbs in 1992.

Much of the indictment, issued by the tribunal in February 1995, relates to events which allegedly occurred at the notorious Omarska prison camp, where Tadic was said by the prosecution to have roamed freely, raping and killing inmates.
The charges carry a maximum punishment of life imprisonment.

Dozens of witnesses said they had seen Tadic help round up Moslems in his home town of Kozarac, but few of those who testified in open court actually witnessed some of the more grisly crimes of which he has been accused.
During the seven-month trial, defence lawyers sought to prove that Tadic was the victim of mistaken identity or of a conspiracy by Moslems to frame him.
The prosecution suffered two major setbacks when one witness to an alleged atrocity in Omarska decided not to testify and another confessed to having lied.

Tadic's defence lawyer Michail Wladimiroff said after the trial the prosecutors had relied soley on uncorroborated evidence from Moslem victims of the Bosnian conflict to portray his client as a "stereotypical bloodthirsty Serb."
He added: "Such a prosecution is doomed to failure."
This will be the second verdict issued by the tribunal.
The first concerned Drazan Erdemovic, a 25-year-old Croat who admitted to taking part in the Bosnian Serb Army massacre of over 1,200 unarmed Moslems at Srebrenica in 1995.
The court sentenced him to 10 years in jail in the first punishment meted out by an international war crimes tribunal since the Nuremburg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.
A third trial, involving three Moslems and a Croat, began in March and is still in its early stages.
The U.N. tribunal has so far indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs (one of whom has since died), 18 Croats and three Moslems.
The two most prominent indicted suspects are former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadic and his military commander Ratko Mladic, both of whom remain at large.
